Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. Assuming the fact that strangers to this country, occupying high places, should not take advantage of the prestige attached to their name . or to their situation to try to influence members of this House of Commons or of a committee of this house on a decision pertaining to Canadian problems now under study, I wish to protest against the statement made yesterday in Halifax by the newly appointed British Ambassador to Washington, Lord Inverchapel, who expressed his preference as to the choice of a national flag for Canada.
Owing to the nature of his statement, and of the reflection it may bear on some of the members of the flag committee, which is sitting this afternoon at four o'clock, I definitely object to this very untimely intervention in such a controversial matter which concerns Canadians and Canadians only.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Interpretation Act, the Bills of Exchange Act and the Civil Service Act provide that the king's birthday, or the day fixed by proclamation for the celebration of the birthday of the reigning sovereign, shall be a public holiday under these statutes. The actual date of His Majesty's birthday is December 14, but since his accession, the king, recognizing that the actual date is an inconvenient one, as it is only eleven days before Christmas, has been graciously pleased to approve the celebration of his birthday in the month of June. Accordingly, with the approval of His Majesty, a proclamation is being isued fixing Monday, June 10, as the date appointed for the celebration of His Majesty's birthday in Canada in 1946.

Explain-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Speaker, this bill is an incident of the comprehensive proposals concerning redistribution expressed in the resolution standing on the order paper to-day.in the name of the Prime Minister. In 1912 parliament provided for the extension of the boundaries . of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba to take in northern portions. In the bill providing for the extension of the boundaries of Quebec it was provided that the population of the new territory would not be counted for the purpose of ascertaining the number to be divided by sixty-five to determine the unit of representation of the other provinces in the Canadian parliament. Under the proposal expressed in the resolution on the order paper it is suggested that hereafter the unit of population for purposes of representation shall no longer be'the population of Quebec divided by sixty-five but the population of all the provinces of Canada divided by 254 or such lesser number as may be arrived at after providing for provinces where representation will be determined by the number of senators they have in the other house.
As a part of the scheme envisaged by the resolution, these conditions which were inserted in the statute annexing to Quebec the northern territory commonly known as Ungava, will become purposeless. This statute of 1912 had provided that it would come into operation only by proclamation, and would not be proclaimed until there had been concurrent legislation by the legislature of Quebec, and this bill would contain a similar provision. It would propose to do away with that restriction in respect of the population of Quebec, but would also contain a clause providing that it would not become operative until proclaimed and would not be proclaimed until met by concurrent legislation of the legislators of
Quebec Boundaries

Quebec. I might add that no such conditions were expressed in the statutes enlarging the area of Ontario and Manitoba, because there was no similar reason for making any special provision in that regard.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO B.N.A. ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (for the the Prime Minister) moved:
That, whereas by the British North America Act, 1867 it is provided that in respect of representation in the House of Commons the province of Quebec shall have the fixed number of sixty-five members;

Redistribution
And whereas the said Act provides that there shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population as the number sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec:
And whereas the said Act provides for the readjustment of representation on the completion of each decennial census, and that on any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last receding readjustment of the number of mem-ers for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one twentieth part or upwards;
And whereas the effect of the aforesaid provisions has not been satisfactory in that proportionate representation of the provinces according to population has not been maintained;
And whereas it is considered that a more equitable apportionment of members to the various provinces could be effected if readjustment were made on the basis of the population of all the provinces taken as a whole.
A humble address be presented to His Majesty The King in the following words:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Members of the House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that You may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom to be expressed as follows:
An Act to provide for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons of Canada on the basis of the population of Canada; '
Whereas the Senate and House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled have submitted an address to His Majesty praying that His Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a bill to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom for the enactment of the provisions hereinafter set forth,
Be it therefore enacted by the King's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same as follows:
1. Section fifty-one of the British North America Act, 1867, is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor:
51. (1) The number of members of the House of Commons shall be two hundred and fifty-five and the representation of the provinces therein shall forthwith upon the coming into force of this section and thereafter on the completion of each decennial census be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time as the Parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules:
1. Subject as hereinafter provided, there shall be assigned to each of the provinces a number of members computed by dividing the total population of the provinces by two hundred and fifty-four and by dividing the population of each province by the quotient so obtained, disregarding, except as hereinafter in this section provided, the remainder if any, after the said process of division.
2. If the total number of members assigned to all the provinces pursuant to rule one is less than two hundred and fifty-four, additional members shall be assigned to the provinces (one to a province) having remainders in the computation under rule one commencing with the province having the largest remainder and continuing with the other provinces in the order of the magnitude of their respective remainders until the total number of members assigned is two hundred and fifty-four.
_ 3. Notwithstanding anything in this section, if upon completion of a computation under rules one and two, the number of members to be assigned to a province is less than the number of senators representing the said province, rules one and two shall cease to apply in respect of the said province, and there shall be assigned to the said province a number of members equal to the said number of senators.
4.	In the event that rules one and two cease to apply in respect of a province then, for the purpose of computing the number of members to be assigned to the provinces in respect of which rules one and two continue to apply, the total population of the provinces shall be reduced by the number of the population of the province in respect of which rules one and two have ceased to apply and the number two hundred and fifty-four shall be reduced by the number of members assigned to such province pursuant to rule three.
5.	Such readjustment shall not take effect until the termination of the then existing parliament.
(2) The Yukon Territory as constituted by chapter forty-one of the Statutes of Canada, 1901, together with any part of Canada not comprised within a province which may from time to time be included therein by the parliament of Canada for the purposes of representation in parliament, shall be entitled to one member.
2. This act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1946, and the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1943, the British North America Act, 1907, and this Act may be cited together as the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1946.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, during the last
session of this parliament there was a lengthy debate on the redistribution of representation in tlhe House of Commons. It arose on a motion submitted by the hon. member for GharlevoixnSaguenay (Mr. Dorion), when he recalled that in 1943, on a joint address to both houses of parliament, an amendment had been adopted by the parliament of the United Kingdom to the British North America Act making it unnecessary to proceed with the distribution consequent upon the census of 1941 until the session following the cessation of hostilities with the German reich, the kingdom of Italy and the empire of Japan. After referring to this the hon. member moved:
That in the opinion of this bouse the government should conform to the aforesaid resolution and take into immediate consideration the advisability of proceeding during the present session with representation of the provinces in the House of Commons, pursuant to the provisions of the British North America Act.
Redistribution

As I said a minute ago, there was a lengthy debate on the motion. The debate was adjourned at the end of the day, and was not resumed during the session. In the course of the debate I ventured to point out I did not think that the resolution, in the terms in Which it was couched, should be adopted, because it would appear to be a determination by the house that it was the government which provided for redistribution of representation in the House of Commons, whilst in fact it is a matter which is the responsibility of parliament.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) then asked for clarification of that statement. I stated that of course members of the government, as members of parliament, realized that because they did have some control over the disposal of the time of the house, they had greater responsibility than did other hon. members to see to it that readjustment of representation was provided in due course.
Before I sat down the leader of the opposition put two questions to me. He asked first:
Does the minister recognize a responsibility on the part of the Canadian parliament to have redistribution before the next election?
And, secondly:
Will the government say now that thye will be such a redistribution?
I answered the first question immediately in the affirmative-and that without the slightest hesitation. Replying to the second question I said I would hope that the government would take the initiative in having that responsibility of parliament to the people of Canada satisfactorily discharged before another election.
Hon, members will recall that in the speech from the throne at this session His Excellency made this statement:
You will be asked to make provision for the redistribution of representation in the House of Commons.
Hon. members will also recall that when in 1943 the government suggested to the house the adoption of an address to His Majesty asking him to have laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom a bill to postpone the redistribution consequent upon the census of 1941, the reasons stated were that redistribution made on the basis of the British North America Act as it stood, and had been construed by decisions of the courts, would bring about a reduction in the membership of the house from 245 to 238, by reducing by three the representation from Manitoba and by four the representation from Saskatchewan; and that even that would leave a further number of thirteen members, in addition to what would

be the representation of the population in the other provinces, based upon the quota obtained by dividing the population of Quebec by sixty-five.
It was also urged that there had been some displacement of population during the war, that it might not be fair to have a redistribution made at that time and on that basis, and that in those troubled days, when the minds of all Canadians were concentrated upon the problems of the war, it might be unfortunate to precipitate the kind of controversy that would arise out of any attempt to make any change in the constitution, as construed, with respect to distribution of representation.
At the last session of parliament it was urged that the amendment in 1943 made it a duty to proceed with redistribution at the first session following the cessation of hostilities. And, though there might have been some technical question then as to whether or not hostilities had completely ceased, that was not the ground upon which it was decided not to ask parliament at that time, or at that session, to consider the problem.
The matter had given us some concern. I had had it carefully examined by law officers in the department, and they had expressed the opinion that there was a duty to have a redistribution made before another general election, but that the statute did not require that it be proceeded with, at the first session following even the cessation of hostilities; that the effect of the amendment was to make it unnecessary to do so during the life of the last parliament, but did not change the requirements of the statute otherwise. And it was pointed out that, in fact, redistributions consequential upon former decennial censuses had not always by any means been attempted at the first session of parliament following the publication of the returns of these census statistics.
But in accord with, the announcement in the speech from the throne the government has felt it should take the initiative of placing the problem before the house, and of asking that it be dealt with at this session. Thereupon the question arose as to whether or not it would be proper to proceed in the same manner and with the same consequences as would have resulted from a redistribution in 1943, or whether it would be preferable to submit to the house a proposal for readjusting the representation on a basis that would not have the consequences to which I have alluded, in the matter of inconsistencies between the population and the number of members sitting in the house.
The government has come to the conclusion , to recommend to parliament the adoption of a petition to His Majesty to cause a bill to

Redistribution
be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to provide for the repeal of section 51 of the British North America Act as it now stands and to substitute therefor the provisions which are printed on pages 4 and 5 of the Routine Proceedings of this day. I do not think it is necessary to take the time of the house to read the text of section 51 as it exists. I think that text is familiar to all members of the house, who know that it provides that Quebec shall have a fixed representation of sixty-five members and that the number of members to be elected by the population of each of the other provinces shall be determined by dividing the population of Quebec by sixty-five to get a quotient and by using that quotient to divide the population of the other provinces.
If that were done, and if that were all that was provided for in the constitution, the result would be that Prince Edward Island would have two members; Nova Scotia would have eleven; New Brunswick would have nine; Quebec, of course, would have the fixed number of sixty-five; Ontario would have seventy-four instead of eighty-two; Manitoba would have fourteen instead of seventeen as at present; Saskatchewan would have seventeen instead of twenty-one; Alberta would have sixteen instead of seventeen; British Columbia would have sixteen as it has at present, and the Yukon would have one because of the special provision made in that regard.
But there are two qualifications of the application of that general rule. One, introduced by way of amendment in 1915, provides that the representation in the House of Commons of a province will never be of a smaller number than that province is entitled to have members of the senate. That provision makes it impossible for the representation of Prince Edward Island to fall below four, because the constitution provides that Prince Edward Island is entitled to have four representatives in the senate. It makes it impossible for the representation of New Brunswick to fall below ten, because that province is entitled to ten senators.
The second qualification, which has existed from the year of origin of the British North America Act in 1867, provides that on any redistribution the representation of a province shall not be diminished unless the proportion which its population bears to the population of the whole of Canada has been reduced by not less than one-twentieth since the last readjustment of its representation in the House of Commons. That provision gave rise to no difficulty until the turn of the century.
63260-122	,
At the turn of the century the application of section 51, even with the qualification, meant a reduction in the representation of Prince Edward Island. The attorney general of that province suggested that under a proper construction of the statute it could not be said that there had been any readjustment in the representation of the people of a province in the House of Commons until the number originally fixed by the constitution had been increased, that until it had been increased there could not be said to have been any readjustment, and that as the representation of the province of Prince Edward Island had never been increased beyond the six which it was at the time of the entry of the province into confederation, there had never been any readjustment and that there could not be any until such time as its population gave it an increase over six.
That argument was submitted to the supreme court and the decision of the court was against the validity of the argument. An appeal was taken to the privy council, and in the case of the Attorney General of the province of Prince Edward Island and the Attorney General of the Dominion of Canada, reported in Law Reports Appeal Cases, 1905, at page 37 and following, it was decided that on a true construction of the British North America Act the argument of the representatives of the Province of Prince Edward Island was unfounded. The language used, and which is to be found at page 51, was this:
This argument assumes that there has been no readjustment for any province unless there has been an alteration. Their Lordships think this is to give too narrow a meaning to the word. In their opinion, when as the result of a census the representation of the provinces is reconsidered and the necessary changes, if any, made to bring it into harmony with the results of the census, that is a readjustment within the meaning of subsection 4, whether there be or be not any change in the case of any particular province.
That decision of the privy council is to be regarded as a binding construction of section 51, subsection 4, of the British North America Act as it now stands. The effect is that unless there has been a diminution of one-twentieth in the proportion of the population of a province to the population of the dominion between two censuses there shall be no change in its representation in the House of Commons. Although since the number of representatives of the province of Ontario was fixed at eighty-two, there has been a diminution in the proportion of more than one-twentieth, it has no effect on the application of the statute because it has not come about within one decade. However, in the case's of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, even
Redistribution

though there has been perhaps a smaller reduction in the proportion of their population to that of the dominion than is at present the case in Ontario since the number of its representatives was changed, there has to be a change because the diminution has come within a decade instead of being spread over more than a decade.
The matter was discussed when the suggestion was made to parliament to adopt an address praying for a postponement of redistribution by way of an amendment to be enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom. At this stage I shall not attempt to comment upon its validity or otherwise but will merely refer to it as a fact.
As was stated by Mr. Newcombe, who argued the case for the dominion in the supreme court, and whose most interesting argument, as [DOT] Were all his arguments, is reported at full length in volume 33, Supreme Court Reports, this could go on indefinitely. You could have a situation growing over a long enough period where the representation of Quebec would remain at sixty-five, although its population might have become considerably larger than that of the premier province of Ontario, which would still be entitled to retain its eighty-two representatives.
Dissatisfaction has been expressed over this growing gap between the original principle of representation by population and the way the provisions of the British North America Act as construed in this Prince Edward Island decision have worked out, and it was felt by the government, in considering the proposals which it should submit to parliament for the readjustment of representation, that a fairer basis for the representation in parliament would be the population of all the provinces as a whole rather than the population of any one province.
Consideration had been given to taking as the basis the population of the province having the largest representation, and dividing that by 82, because it so happens that 82 is the number of members that Ontario had in the first parliament of Canada. It grew from 82 to 92 and is now back to 82. But it was found that that would not work out entirely satisfactorily, and it was found that it was perhaps not fair to any province to have it in such a position that any necessary reduction in its representation would be attributable to what had happened in the pivotal province. It was thought that it would be fairer to the population of the whole country to have the growth of the country, taken as a whole, determine the representation in the House of Commons, rather than to have the growth in 
any one locality applied generally throughout the whole country. The proposal which it is submitted it would be proper to request the parliament of the United Kingdom to substitute for the method now in effect is that the representation be fixed at 255; that the Yukon territory, and such other portions of lands as are not now within the limits of any province as parliament may at any time see fit to annex to the Yukon territory for purposes of representation, have one member; that the population of all the provinces of Canada be then divided by 254 to obtain a quotient, and that that quotient serve as a divisor of the population of each province separately; and that if as a result of that operation it should happen 'that any one or more provinces would have a lesser number allocated to it than its numbers in the senate, then that rule would be disregarded for that province and it would have allotted to it the number of representatives in the House of Commons equal to the number by which it is entitled to be represented in the senate; and that the 254 would be reduced by the number that is allocated to the province to which the rule no longer applied; and that the population of the other provinces would be divided by 254 less that number.
In the present circumstances the calculation made in that way would show that Prince Edward Island would receive only two representatives, and that being less than its number of senators the proposal requires that it be allotted four representatives; that the population of the other eight provinces together be divided by 250, and that the quotient thus arrived at serve to divide the population of all the other provinces.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is what happened the last time.
Another question, which has arisen each time there has been any move to ask for an amendment of the British North America Act, has been whether or not the provinces had been consulted and had agreed to it. I think that when the question is put in that form it is ambiguous. The provinces, that is to say the people of the provinces, are all represented in this parliament, and for the purposes of such matters as are confided to the jurisdiction of this parliament it is by those representatives here that the people of the provinces speak. There are other matters given by the act to the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures and the provincial governments; with respect to any of those it is my view that it would not be possible to deal with them without the consent of those to whose jurisdiction they have been confided. My view of the confederation enactment-it matters little whether it be called a pact or any other name-is that there was an assembly of distinguished' gentlemen representing in the conferences four colonial legislatures, legislatures which legislated by delegation of the parliament of the United Kingdom; so much so that if one looks at the constitution of 1791, the parliaments then set up for Lower Canada and for Upper Canada were expressly authorized to enact laws for the peace, order and good government of these colonies. It was expressly provided that those laws would be obligatory by virtue of the enactment of the parliament of the empire, and practically the same language was conserved in the act of union between the two Canadas in 1840. Then the representatives of the people which had legislatures of that delegated character met and discussed resolutions which were finally submitted to the imperial parliament for enactment, and by those resolutions they provided that the sum total of the sovereignty would be divided between two jurisdictions; one portion would go to the central parliament, another portion would go to the provincial legislatures; and the courts have held that with respect to what was allocated to the provincial legislatures they are not mandatories or agents of or subservient to the central parliament; they have received that portion of the sovereignty of the nation to exercise it under their own sovereign authority; and it is my view that nothing which has thus been allocated to them can be taken from them without their participation. They have been given exclusive jurisdiction over that field, and it cannot be interfered with. But on the other hand, exclusive jurisdiction over other matters was given to the other representative body of the Canadian people,

Redistribution
and it so happens that the representation in this house has to be adjusted from time to time in such manner and subject to such conditions as this parliament, composed of the representatives of all the provinces, determines.
When I hear these suggestions that the constitution of the Canadian parliament results from a delegation made by these original colonial legislatures I sometimes wonder how that can be seriously argued, when it is remembered that at the time the two groups of population with respect to which the argument is urged so forcibly are the group of Anglo-Saxon descent and the group of French descent. At that time they were both in one legislature, and their representatives appointed by that one legislature participated in the conference which led to the enactment of the statute of 1867. It seems inconceivable to me that John A. Macdonald, afterwards Sir John A. Macdonald, was not as much a representative of the group for which he spoke before the first of July, 1867, after confederation had been proclaimed, as he was the representative of that group in the various conferences that took place prior thereto. And similarly that George Etienne Cartier, afterwards Sir George Etienne Cartier, was not as much a representative of the group for whom he spoke and negotiated in the Quebec conference after the proclamation of the statute of 1867 as he was before that time.
These are matters about which one must be rather careful. I know there is no desire anywhere to do anything that is not in accord with the true spirit and intent that presided over these deliberations; but it is apt to appear a bit strange to have it constantly urged that for the purposes of any amendment whatsoever to the British North America Act the persons who are competent to express opinions are the provincial legislatures. They are competent to express opinions on all matters allocated in the statute to provincial jurisdiction; but as to everything that was put within central jurisdiction by the statute of 1867, the statute provided how the people were to be represented and to what assembly His Majesty and his constitutional advisers were to be responsible.
This matter of adjusting representation is something which in express terms falls to be determined by the parliament of Canada. Of course there are rules expressed in the section which can be modified only by the legislative body which enacted them. Section 51 of the original act provided that:
On the completion of the census in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces-
By virtue of the decision expressly made by the supreme court and the privy council in the Prince Edward Island case, that has to be read "the representation of all the provinces." I continue:
-shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides,-
Subject to the subsections expressed. It is the parliament of Canada, subject to such action as may be taken by the parliament of the United Kingdom, which is the only body having been given jurisdiction in that regard in 1867. And under the Statute of Westminster it is now provided that the parliament of the United Kingdom will not act in respect of Canadian affairs except upon request. According to constitutional practice that request has to be expressed in the form of humble addresses presented to His Majesty.
As to whether or not it is proper at this time that there should be a modification made that would provide for a truly proportionate representation based on population, it is for this house to decide on this resolution. There can be no doubt that the time will come when the application of these restrictive rules will become unbearable. The general principle is representation according to population. There will come a time-there cannot be any doubt about that-when anything that gets seriously out of line with that principle will be considered unbearable. In this house there are twenty representatives who are not here because there is behind them the quotient provided for by the general rule. In my opinion that is sufficient to make it desirable to get back to a rule which will provide for a truly proportionate distribution of the representatives in this house. Should it be 255; should it be 245, or 238? These are matters of detail. But it so happens that by making it 255 there seems to be at this time only one province which will see its representation diminished, and there it will be diminished by only one.
It is a matter of practical experience, I think, that it is always painful to bring about a readjustment which requires a diminution in representation. It does not seem to me that a house composed of 255 members would be inordinately large, not only in view of the numbers of our population but in view of the immense territory the representatives in this house represent. Do we always realize that the area of this country is enormous-from one ocean to the other, from the boundaries of the United States to the north pole, an area scarcely smaller than the whole of Europe and somewhat larger than the whole of the United States? Of course, were it not for the

Redistribution
fact that only a relatively small fraction of it is regarded as potentially valuable for agricultural purposes, it would be difficult to explain why there are only twelve million people in that vast area; but the representation is territorial, and the territory is very large.
I submit that there should be found much to commend itself to hon. members in this proposal, which will provide, if it is adopted, that hereafter the adjustment of representation will be in accord with the general growth all over the country from one ocean to the other and from the United States border to the north pole. And whenever in applying the results brought about by the growth over the whole country it does happen that one province suffers some diminution in its representation, it will not be chargeable to happenings in any other individual province.

When the committee rose a week ago last Friday evening I was speaking to this item, and was pointing out that there had been reports of abortions occurring in herds that had been vaccinated. In that connection I should like to quote one paragraph from an article sent out by the Ontario Veterinary college at Guelph. It deals with the duration of immunity, and states:
The interval of time during which the resistance against infection lasts has not been definitely established. Outbreaks amongst adult vaccinated animals, vaccinated three to six years previously, have been reported. The question of revaccination in such instances is under survey at the present time. The duration of immunity therefore, has not been definitely fixed.
A considerable amount of work is being done along these lines at the Ontario Veterinary college. The paragraph does bring up the point as to how long after initial treatment the animals should be revaccinated. Abortions have occurred in vaccinated animals from six to eight years after, and in this instance from nine to ten years after the vaccination of the herds. This fact may lead farmers to believe that vaccination is not a proper procedure, and I suggest that veterinarians who are doing vaccinating work should reassure the farmers who may have questioned this process. It should be pointed out that vaccination is not a cure, and was never intended to be. It does however have a worthwhile restraining effect upon the recurrence of the disease.
Many breeders have felt that the disease would be contracted from vaccinated animals.
I tried to point out last fall that this was not so, and in that connection I would read another paragraph from the same report, which deals with the subject of the stability of strain 19. It says:
The strain has been injected into pregnant females, producing abortion. These animals inoculated, have been free of infection prior to the next pregnancy. Furthermore, contact normal pregnant females did not contract the disease. The germ, when re-isolated, or recovered

from these experimental animals, had the same qualities as the original strain 19. Hence, the strain 19 is stable.
Now, as further evidence of the fallacy of this programme as now carried on by the department, I should like to quote from the North American Veterinarian of April, 1944, where it says:
For fifteen years, the blood-test method for the control of brucellosis in cattle has been given the most earnest and efficient support by the vast majority of veterinarians, state sanitary control officials and cattle-breeders. Few disease-control measures have had as much trial or have ever been given greater financial or professional support. This method has been of value in keeping many herds free from infection as far as could be determined by the agglutination test. How-ever, such herds are in constant danger from some undisclosed, latent infection or from infection gaining entrance to the herd from the outside.
In areas where herds are small and cattle are few in number, the disease incidence is reduced and the problem of control is vastly simplified.
The ultimate control and eradication of the disease in areas where herds are large and in close proximity and where the rate of infection is heavy, becomes a problem of considerable magnitude. In such areas control and eradication by the testing method alone has in many instances resulted in almost complete eradication of the herd, not only once, but several times.
I should like to emphasize that last sentence. To continue:
After the most thorough and conscientious efforts were expended over a period of years, the more farsighted practising veterinarians and cattle-breeders concluded that this method, even though bolstered by huge state and federal funds, would not accomplish the desired end.
And further down:
Considerable progress of a more permanent nature in the control of brucellosis in cattle in Illinois and throughout the country has been made during the past few years.
And again:
Cattle breeders and veterinarians have found that calfhood vaccination has given them an offensive weapon with which to fight the disease and in recent years definite progress has been made at a minimum of expense. Veterinarians realize that this procedure is not 100 per cent perfect but they have found a method that has enabled them to make permanent gains-a method that has enabled cattle breeders to plan their breeding operations with greater security and confidence.
I should like to say a word about the action taken by the Ontario Veterinary college at Guelph, and to commend the Ontario department of agriculture for the action it has taken; because as far as I know Ontario is the only province that has taken a definite stand on this matter. The Ontario Veterinary college has made available vaccine for all breeders in the province. The vaccine will be distributed through the agency of qualified veterinarians. Vaccine will be maintained in

Supply-Agriculture
the fresh state and will be distributed free of charge. The breeders will be responsible for the payment for the injection of vaccine. The college will supply the veterinarian with the vaccine, vaccination certificate forms and ear tags. During the present year the college plans to make the programme provincer-wide in its application.
I hope I have made my point quite clear. Action must be taken for the protection not only of the cattle breeders of this country but of human life as well. As I have said before, this disease probably causes more loss to cattle breeders than any other disease we know of, and it will continue to cause large losses unless something definite is done.
There are two other types of this disease, one affecting swine and the other affecting goats. The one affecting swine is known as brucella suis and the one affecting goats as brucella melitensis. They say that in some parts of the United States seventy per cent of the undulant fever in humans is caused by brucella suis. This disease is very difficult to diagnose in swine because abortions are not noticeable. For this reason brucella suis is far more important from the human standpoint than the brucella abortus which affects cattle. I should like to quote Veterinary Medicine of March, 1946, page 99, as follows:
On the whole, it is not the economic loss from swine brucellosis but the public health aspect that is most important. In the whole country there is a large number of cases of undulant fever in man, and the incidence is increasing year by year. What percentage of these cases is due to the porcine type of the organism is not known, but statistics gathered in Iowa, the leading state in swine production, shows 75 per cent of the eases to be due to the suis type. Curiously enough, in Alabama, which is not an important swine producing state, a survey showed almost the same percentage-72 per cent-of the cases of undulant fever to be due to the swine organism. Every epidemic of undulant fever that has occurred in this country, so far, has been due to the suis type of the organism, in most, perhaps all instances due to the infection of cattle and contamination of raw milk with the swine type of the organisms.
I think we have much to learn in this country regarding this organism and I suggest that the Department of Agriculture get in touch with the United States officials and find out all they can about it. As I said, it is important not only as it affects the cattle breeders, but also because of its possible effect upon the health of this nation.

I rise with some hesitation to take part in a discussion upon so specialized a matter as testing for Bang's disease and tuberculosis in cattle and other animals, but I should like to relate to the committee an incident which came to my notice during the 63260-123
week-end. It was brought to my attention by the farmer concerned', and he was in the gathering where there were others to testify to the facts in the matter. This farmer had an accredited and listed herd of Holsteins, which is the term used in connection with the dominion government testing programme. His herd numbered some forty-four cattle. During the last twelve years he has never had a positive reaction. Tests should have been made last November, but there, was some delay caused by congestion brought about by the war. The tests were made two or three weeks ago, and every one of his forty-four cattle went down. There was one calf which escaped but they took the calf off with the rest to the abattoir. The farmer tells me that in this instance a new serum was used for testing ' purposes. Whether it is more sensitive or not I dio not know; in any event the result has been very strange, as I think the minister will agree. This farmer can ill afford the loss of his herd. I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that when the cattle went to Swift's abattoir for slaughtering, particular attention was paid to these animals by those specializing in the making of tests when animals are killed, and not a single bit of evidence of tuberculosis was found in the whole herd. This serves only to arouse further suspicion in the minds of the farming community in which this man lives. In fact it is causing consternation, because the farmers feel that either the new serum must have been too sensitive or there must have been some error in making the test. The farmers are inclined to attribute it to the new serum, and oppose any suggestion that the test was not properly carried out.
I shall give the minister the farmer's name and address, and his lot and1 concession number-he does not happen to be in my constituency-so that he may make an investigation. It is a matter of grave concern to the fanning community, and -the sooner a full explanation is made from the ministerial level the better it will be for all concerned. An investigation should be instituted and the truth be made known so that rumours will not be flying about such as I heard over the weekend.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the first place I wish to thank the hon. member for Peel for having brought this matter before the committee. The facts are very much as they have been stated so far as tuberculin is concerned. The reason for introducing the new tuberculin some four or five months ago was that our cattle going across into the United

Supply-Agriculture

States and being tested with this tuberculin were going down, and that was having a very bad effect on the trade of our breeding stock going into the United States. So the department decided to use the same tuberculin that was being used in the United States. There are some cattle going down under the test of this tuberculin., which did not go down under the tuberculin that was used before. Apparently it has a more sensitive reaction, but so far as we have been able to determine up to the moment it does not result in cattle going down that are not affected by tuberculosis. Of course the object of these tests is to get all the cattle that are affected. It is just possible that cattle which were reacting negatively under the old test are going down under the test with this new tuberculin. It is just as well that the question should be discussed here and information given to the committee in regard to it.
The department is making a most careful check to make sure that no undue hardship is being caused to anyone as a result of the use of this new tuberculin. I am sure that all breeders, particularly those breeding for sale outside Canada, will desire to have their market retained by having the most careful check made of animals on this side.

May I ask what have been the results in the last five or six months since this new tuberculin was introduced? Have there been similar cases to the one I have discussed this afternoon, in which whole herds which for years have been reacting negatively to the old test have gone down under the new test?

We have no information up to the moment as to a whole herd reacting negatively under the old test and then, with one exception, reacting positively under the new test. There are no such cases on record. There are cases of individual animals reacting negatively under the old test and positively under the new test. That was the reason for using this serum. Our cattle were reacting negatively under the old test and were reacting positively to the new serum on the other side of the line. The complaint was made that animals afflicted with tuberculosis were being shipped into the United States even though we were giving certificates that they were free from the disease.
I do not know that I should attempt to give a detailed explanation of the different methods by which the tuberculin is developed, but this serum is being .used in the United States, where our greatest market is, and to protect the breeder here we thought we should use the same tuberculin.

I would ask the minister to clear up one more point which the farmers have made to me. At the abattoir where the cattle were slaughtered the veterinaries

I suppose they would be veterinaries-
They would be veterinaries.

The veterinaries found no evidence of tuberculosis in this herd. Would1 a veterinary at the abattoir, after a cow had been declared to have reacted positively, be able to find evidence of tuberculosis in the animal?
That would not be definite proof that the animal was not affected, because the disease cannot always be detected in the slaughtering.

It seems strange that forty-four of them had been declared negative and then were declared positive under this new test, and yet not one of them showed any evidence of tuberculosis at the abattoir. This has confirmed the suspicions of the farming community in which this man lives and carries on his business. I would ask the minister to make a personal investigation of the case I have brought to his attention.
If my hon. friend will give me the name and all particulars, we shall go into the case.
I shall be glad to do .that.

May I ask the minister if there are manjr municipalities in Manitoba which have made requests for the tuberculin test which it has been found impossible to accede to? In one area I have in mind, the farmers, mostly very good farmers, are raising splendid cattle, but they are isolated, and while all the municipalities surrounding them have had the test, this municipality has not been able to get one because of the shortage of veterinaries. Thus they are placed at a great disadvantage in the distribution of their herds, and they are hoping for a remedy very soon. I know that the trouble has been the shortage of veterinaries, and I would ask the minister whether there is a likelihood of the situation correcting itself in the near future.

There are six municipalities in Manitoba which have been accepted but have not yet been passed. A number of others-I have not here the figures as to the exact numbers

have made applications which have not yet been finally considered, but six have been accepted but the tests have not yet been made. The reason for that is

Supply-Agriculture
largely a lack of veterinarians to make the tests. But there are some isolated cases where applications have been made and where it is not intended to make the tests right away. I would take it that a case which would be in the vicinity of Brandon would be in a block, rather than isolated. Efforts" are being made to make the test as far as possible in all the areas where there is a block of municipalities around about which have already been accepted and where tests have been started but not completed.

A few years ago a test was taken in a number of municipalities, and I understand that it must be continued over a period of several years before it becomes authentic. That is, we do not accept those plants as plants from which meat can be exported, either interprovincially or internationally. But in certain provinces there may be meat sold which has been put up within the province by a plant that we do not inspect, so I cannot say definitely that all meat condemned in Montreal or Toronto or somewhere else has been inspected by us. We inspect at the plant where the product is being put up for export from one province to another or for export from this country to another country.
The way I understand it is that if the meat is only to be sold within the province you do not have to inspect it.

size, that will not bring their plants up to the standard we require: they do not intend to export meat, and therefore, they say, we are going along under provincial regulations as they are, or probably under the health regulations of the city in which they operate. Will sufficient grain be available in the west to supply the eastern provinces with feed for their hogs and chickens this year? I have been attempting during the whole session, and as a matter of fact since before the session opened, to emphasize the fact that feed supplies are low, not only in eastern Canada but all across the dominion. The reason they are low in different parts of the country is that they are low at the source from which the feed is obtained, that is, the prairie provinces, and at present the position for the future is not too encouraging. The crop is not going in under the best of conditions, and I am not in a position to say whether or not farmers will be able to obtain the full amount of feed they may require to finish, their live stock. That is something individual farmers will be able to determine much better than anyone here. The fact is that the supply is

low, and it is low partly because we have had comparatively poor crops during the last two years, one year getting a little poorer than the year preceding. The other reason is that people are to-day insisting on farmers placing upon the market all cereals available for human consumption. We think in terms of wheat When we think of consuming cereals in this country, but in other countries they want any kind of cereal at all. They simply say that it takes five to eight pounds of barley or oats to produce a pound of pork or beef, and they go on, "Give us the barley and oats for the present." So we are shipping it out.
Just a short time ago, in the last announcement he made in connection with this campaign, the Prime Minister stated that we had undertaken to ship practically all the feed wheat we had left in Canada for human consumption in Europe, and that at the same time we had undertaken to send five million bushels of oats. I rise as one of the representatives of one of the geographically favoured parts of Canada, southwestern Ontario, comprising the counties of Huron, Lambton, Middlesex, Elgin, Kent and Essex. This portion is geographically favoured, as our latitude of 42 degrees-it will be seen by tracing it out on the map-is the same as that of a large part of the well known state of California. It is often said that this area is the banana belt of Canada, and though we do not grow bananas, our soil and climate are such as to make this a highly productive region for many of the well known and specially favoured canning fruits and vegetables with which we are all so familiar. The composition of the soil is similar to that of the great agricultural states of Illinois, Ohio and Indiana, and our climate being on the border-line of the warm southern states and the colder northern parts of Canada brings us a great variety of insect pests and plant diseases peculiar to both the hot and the colder geographical regions of North America.
The existence of some 20,000 types of insects that may have an injurious effect on the crops of this area is a hazard that cannot and must not be overlooked. The estimated value of this highly productive area in 1943 was $99 million, and the estimated loss from insect pests was eight per cent, or approximately $8 million. This is a staggering loss, not only in monetary value, but in food, which at present is so urgently needed. Since this area, in conjunction with the rest of Canada, is exhorted to produce as we never produced before, we are bringing this matter before the department for its utmost consideration, asking its greatest assistance by way of supplying trained men to help the farmers combat .these pests, and thereby overcoming this farm loss.
It is true that our farmers are doing all they can to carry out the methods as recommended to them by departmental experts, but in spite of this we are waging a losing battle. Our clover crop, one of our best winter feeds and soil builders, for reasons entirely unknown, is decreasing year by year. Our exacting methods of farming require a clover crop in our rotation cycle, and we cannot afford to lose it.
Our preferred list of field crops, including tobacco, sugar beets, soya beans, vegetables, fruit crops and field beans, all suffer from important and urgent disease conditions. These are in addition to and far removed from the above-mentioned insect pests.
Supply-Agriculture

The farmer, with a layman's limitations, is in the unhappy position where having done all he can do, he still faces the possibility of either complete loss of a vital crop, or an annual loss of staggering proportions.
Since, in this area, we are asked to plant and cultivate 35,000 acres of sugar beets this year, and since, to date, some 26,000 acres have been contracted for, it is urgent that I again bring to the attention of the committee a disastrous plan disease called a nemotode, which is seriously affecting this plant in as yet certain defined areas. But its ravages are spreading. This same nematode is what created such havoc in the sugar beet area of Utah. The entomologists of the Department of Agriculture are well aware of its existence, its ravages and its menace and have made some surveys concerning it; but as yet no complete eradication action has been taken.
The field bean crop is one of great importance because it comprises a large acreage and is a favoured crop in all this area, since some
58,000	acres were reported as of 1942, with noticeable increases in the succeeding war years. Although this acreage may look small to our western wheat growers who compute their acreage in the millions, it was nevertheless a valuable food contribution in our war effort, and was a substantial cash crop to the hard-worked farmer. It requires much attention during the growing and harvesting periods, and scientific skill is required for its successful completion. In addition to the insect pests that attack it, it is also subjected to a plant disease called the fusarium wilt, which as yet is an undetermined disease.
A disease peculiar and injurious to our corn crop is the ear and stock rot. Those peculiar to the tobacco crop are black root rot, brown root rot, blue mould, seedling diseases, and leaf spots. The soya bean is also not lacking in plant diseases, because it is subject to virus diseases, pod and stem blight, and fusarium wilt.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister at this time further to magnify the farmer's drawbacks and difficulties, and also his dependence on the Department of Agriculture for their trained and scientific assistance and knowledge in combating and overcoming his great drawbacks and difficulties.
Excellent work is being .done by the dominion laboratory of plant pathology at Harrow, but here again the staff and facilities available are not sufficient to cope with the many diseases affecting these vital crops.
In addition to the laboratory at Harrow, the dominion government has set up a dominion entomological laboratory at Chatham. These laboratories have been doing

excellent work, but the needs are so increasingly great that an enlarged service is necessary. It is appreciated that there is great difficulty in obtaining greater numbers of highly trained personnel, larger buildings, and more equipment to study the origin and control of these insect pests and plant diseases which are playing such havoc. But it is considered that the potential hazards are so great that no effort on the part of this department should be spared in attracting personnel to the fields of pathology and entomology, and also in obtaining the buildings and equipment so necessary for the carrying out of their scientific work.
It is recommended that the dominion entomological laboratory at Chatham and the dominion laboratory of plant pathology at Harrow be expanded to meet present and anticipated future requirements.
The department has recognized our requirements by setting up these two stations to study plant diseases and insects. All of us from that part of the country join in asking for further support. I notice that in the estimates this year there is an extra $89,662 for that particular branch of agriculture, but I exhort the minister on behalf of those six townships for a just and equitable share so that we may carry on as we should like to.

production of explosives under arrangements made with the British and French governments and this plant can supply the nitrates necessary for the production of fertilizers. I do not want to be misunderstood. My information is that if we could utilize the Calgary plant wholly or even partly for the production of fertilizers there would be an advantage in operating that plant. We did not lightly dispose of the plant. The Canadian federation of agriculture approached me a year ago to inquire about the possibilities of the government operating the plant. We examined all the factors, and the results of the investigation were such as I have just stated.
When it was apparent that the government would not be interested in operating the plant I got in touch with the pools in western Canada and suggested that they investigate the matter to determine whether or not farm organizations might be interested in operating the plant. The result was that no one desired to assume the responsibility of operating the plant under all the circumstances and with all the information available. It was not thought, because of the amount of money which would have to be invested, that the plant could be operated as a separate unit by either the farm organizations, the provincial government or the federal Department of Agriculture.
As a matter of fact I made application on one occasion on behalf of the federal Department of Agriculture For full information with a view to our operating it for the advantage of the farmers. After obtaining all the the information, I came to the conclusion that those who were advising against it were probably more correct than I if I insisted upon having the plant operated by the Department of Agriculture as an operation separate from the other operations in Canada.

I understood the minister to say that the plant at Galgary would eventually be closed.

I did not intend to say that. My understanding is that the plant at Calgary was sold to Consolidated Smelters and I assume that they will operate it. I was attempting to show that the plant in the east can be operated by the government to do two jobs, and the department concerned did not feel that they could successfully operate the Calgary plant along with the other one which would have to be operated in any event. They argued that the Calgary plant should be sold to the highest bidder. I attempted to have the farm organizations put in a bid. I do not think the plant will be closed down, although its operations have been reduced. Before I left home at Easter I know there was considerable difficulty in getting fertilizer there. I was unable to understand why that was so, because the plant had been converted for some time to the production of fertilizer. Especially was it difficult for the returned man to get fertilizer from the plant at Calgary. In fact I had to get in touch with the manager personally to obtain fertilizer for veterans. The supply was so short that a certain amount was allotted to each district and the farmers were not given the amount they required.
Was that in Alberta?

Yes. Farm organizations throughout the whole district had put in their orders and the general policy of the plant was-and this is what I took exception to- that no returned man could be given fertilizer until the orders from these farm organizations had been filled. Another difficulty was that

a returned man could not get fertilizer unless he had purchased it the year before. They were fighting the year before, and when they came back from the battlefield to the farm they found they could not get fertilizer. No relief was given until I personally telephoned the manager in one or two cases, and he was good enough to take the matter up and see that they did get fertilizer.
The Whole point I want to make is that the amount of fertilizer being -produced in Canada is not sufficient to supply the local demand. If the minister had thoroughly investigated the whole situation before turning down the idea of taking over the Calgary plant, which was not producing at full capacity, he would have found that the supply was not beginning to meet the demand for fertilizer. If the supply is short in Alberta it must be short in Saskatchewan and, I would think, in Manitoba too. If this plant were producing at capacity .it would be of great assistance to agriculture and incidentally the company would be making a profit. I cannot explain why they are not producing enough to supply the demand unless they consider that in two or three years the demand will drop off and that therefore it would not pay them to go into greater production. Certainly at the present time the demand for fertilizer far exceeds the supply, and I think the minister would be well advised to investigate to see what can be done to expand the production of fertilizer.

The plant at Calgary does not produce fertilizer, but nitrates. Nitrates are not used to any great extent in producing fertilizer in western Canada. They are used to mix with other ingredients in producing fertilizer. If we were to operate the plant at Calgary to capacity it would supply all the nitrates that are needed in all Canada and in a considerable part of the United States. It is not a case of operating that plant to get fertilizer. Our information is that fertilizer is available for all the prairie provinces. No shortage has been reported to us from the prairie provinces. There may be certain areas which do not have not their share; I do not know about that, but the report we have is that there is sufficient fertilizer for the prairie provinces.

Technically the minister may be right. The plant itself produces nitrates, and these nitrates may be shipped in some form or another to be made into fertilizer. But there definitely is a plant there for the distribution of fertilizer. I got in touch with the manager to see that these returned men got some fertilizer, and it was quite

evident from the information I got from him that the fertilizer which is being distributed from that particular point is in short supply. I cannot reconcile the minister's statement with the information given to me by the manager because he definitely stated that they did not have a sufficient supply to meet the demand. If a returned man were just starting in on the land he could not get fertilizer because he had not purchased the year before. The only reason he got it was that I interceded with the manager, and he told me that he had to get in touch with the local agent and say to him: "We have allotted you so many tons to fill the orders you have sent in from the farmers around, and you will have available to these returned men." That is how critical the shortage was. The minister should make a further investigation of the situation.

I commend the minister for putting the grant back to $25,000 for the seed growers' association, and I hope he will be able to increase this amount in the supple-mentaries because this association is doing a good job. Last week, when the Minister of Agriculture was in Washington, the following press release appeared in the papers:
LaGuardia raps low wheat price paid in Canada
Criticism was expressed by UNRRA director, F. H. LaGuardia, at the united nations food and agriculture conference Tuesday. He said the nations cannot get away with "squeezing their farmers any more."
Farmers are industry's best customers. President Roosevelt understood this and obtained legislation insuring parity between agriculture and labour.
This, however, has had a great bearing on Canada, resulting in disparities which must be adjusted.
Mr. Gardiner said "Mr. LaGuardia seems to have little knowledge of Canadian economy. There is far greater parity between the incomes of farmers and labour in Canada than there is in the United States."
I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if he was correctly reported. If so, this would be the proper time to give us some facts to substantiate his statement.

I have done that so often during this session that I am afraid I would be wasting the time of the committee to do it again. I doubt if there is anyone in the committee who does not realize that we have better than parity prices in Canada. The situation, however," which was being referred to by Mr. LaGuardia at that time had not to do with wheat. The suggestion made was that he was dicussing the relatively low price of wheat in Canada. What he was really discussing was the general world position in relation to food, and laying before the meeting which was held to discuss that situation the conditions existing in the United States in relation to the matter of food. He did pass the remark, toward the end of his comments, that they had made certain provisions in the United States for parity and that the level of prices in the United States provided for under that arrangement did have some effect on Canada. I do not think his intention was to imply that our prices, being lower than theirs, had any particular effect upon the relationship existing in Canada as between what the farmer paid for necessities and what he obtained for his product. His meaning, I thought, from discussions I had with him afterwards, was that if you are going to maintain one price level on one side of the line and another price level on the other side of the line, difficulties are bound to develop in the course of time because of the differences.

Supply-Agriculture
The newspaper reporter who asked me what I thought about it at the moment got this reply, that "I am quite certain that the greatest difficulty we have in maintaining price levels as between the United States and Canada results from the fact that we have high tariff walls and that one of those is related to wheat." If anyone mentioned wheat in connection with any of the discussions, it was I. I said that there was ho possibility of our ever having the same price level in Canada as in the United States so long as the United States maintained its duty against wheat of forty-two cents a bushel.
I should like to say, now that the question is up, that in my opinion the 42-cent duty on wheat going from Canada into the United States has more to do with the wheat problem throughout the world, both in peace time and during the war than any other one thing. I think, when we are talking about removing obstructions from trade and making it easier for people to assist in feeding one another, one of the first things which ought to be done in some way or another is to have that obstruction removed from the handling of wheat on this continent; and until it is removed there will always be trouble in maintaining price levels as between the United States and this country. That is the remark which I made, and I want to make it here.

Just on that point, the Minister of Labour issued on May 6, a pamphlet setting out the prices of five articles, namely, butter, eggs, sugar, bread and milk, for 1920 as compared with 1946, and indicating a reduction of approximately 46 per cent in prices this year as compared with 1920. But he omitted to state that industrial hourly wages in Canada have increased by over 30 per cent since 1920, which of course is an added injustice to our farmers; and, according to the government's own records, the wages of farm labour between 1939 and January, 1946, have increased by 110-8 per cent.
Other arguments which we have gone through in the past do not need to be repeated. But I may just point out that during the first great war our farmers received 29 per cent of the national income; during the last great war their share of the national income was only 18 per cent; and everybody knows the variation in prices prevailing on both sides of the line for cereals, meat and dairy products. Only the other day I noticed in a Winnipeg newspaper an article wherein the deputy minister of agriculture of Manitoba, in addressing a group of women consumers on the milk problem, stated that never in his recollection of the history of this country had there been so many dairy herds being disposed
of as had occurred this spring in Manitoba. I believe the same state of affairs applies throughout the dominion. The minister has admitted that implements of farm production can be bought cheaper in the United States than in Canada. On the other hand, I am sure that if anybody will take the trouble to go to banks situated a few miles apart in Canada and the United States he will be amazed at the result of a comparison of bank deposits of farmers on the Canadian side and in the United States during the last six years.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few observations on marketing from the point of view of my farmer constituents. We have heard so much from another section of Canadian producers that I think it is about time you listened to representations on behalf of British Columbia farmers. The men with whom I have worked for forty years are not large farmers, but men who have hewn their small farms out of the woods and are more acquainted with the axe, the grub-hoe and the walking-plough than the combines and tractors and rubber-tired machines on which my hon. friends to my right ride around in comfort to do their work. On the whole, the British Columbia farmers find it necessary to work both summer and winter in order to make a living, and I have never seen many of them staying at the Empress hotel in Victoria. But I must say that they are people who have accomplished something, and I am going to put forward their views this evening as the views of people who are not asking the government to do something for them, except to this extent, to provide them with the necessary legal machinery to give them the protection necessary to enable them to work out their own economic salvation.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I am a citizen of no mean village. I can illustrate briefly what has been done by these people in a cooperative way. I come from a village which, with a district covering a radius of ten miles, contains about 750 people. I have been in that district almost since the first tree was chopped down. I have seen every acre cleared; I have seen every orchard planted. These 750 people, representing many races, including the various peoples of Europe and different portions of the British isles, have, as a result of cooperative action, in that time built and paid for their own irrigation system and, although it cost $50,000, do not owe a dollar; it supplies water to these farmers at a dollar each per month. They have built their own nine-hole golf course and recreation grounds at a cost of $10,000 and do not owe a 5-cent
Supply-Agriculture

piece. They have built a community hospital at a cost of $47,000, of which they do not owe a cent. The legion branch in that district, composed of several farmers and farmers' sons, and numbering sixty-seven members, have completed a legion hall worth $15,000 and on which there is not a cent of debt. I mention these facts as an illustration of the . type of cooperative effort that goes on in the district which I represent, and which is general throughout the Kootenay district. These people have put forth a tremendous effort along cooperative lines, and they are simply asking the government to give consideration to a type of legislation which they deem necessary to protect them in the future.
Before proceeding further, I must say that the farmers of my constituency believe that, on the whole, the government has handled the marketing of their major products during the war period in a commonsense way and has, on the whole, met very difficult circumstances satisfactorily. But they are concerned with their position when the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act ceases to operate.
When speaking on the agriculture estimates last session I had this to say, as reported at page 2527 of Hansard:
The farmers of my constituency are particularly interested in three aspects of our agricultural policy: first, marketing arrangements, to assure stable and satisfactory marketing and farm income; second, disease control, to ensure satisfactory crops; and, third, intensive research in the field of marketing problems and disease control.
That is their opinion at the present time. In the provincial field we have a satisfactory natural products marketing act; in the international field we have the food and agriculture organization of the united nations and the latent possibilities of world agricultural councils, but in between we maintain there is a missing link, namely, a national natural products marketing act that will tie together provincial and international arrangements.
I know something of the pioneer days in the fruit industry. In the early days of this century, as most hon. members know, settlers flocked into the interior of British Columbia, settlers without experience on the whole. As a result of their appreciation of the possibilities of cooperation and its practice, they have built one of the outstanding cooperative movements in the British empire and in the fruit industry as a whole in the world.
In recent year? I have often heard it said that the pioneering spirit of the Canadian people is dead; but I do not believe this, nor do those who are associated with me. I believe it is simply a question now of channeling that spirit into new fields of social

adventure and economic organization. Fruit growers of British Columbia believe that the time is ripe to pioneer a national natural products marketing act. For the information of the members, so that they will get this picture clearly, may I give a brief history of the development of the fruit industry and the marketing arrangements in British Columbia. It is a romance of collective effort, disappointments, failures and final success, worthy of careful study by all who are interested in the various aspects of cooperative endeavour. In the interior the fruit growing sections of British Columbia are located chiefly in the Okanagan from Armstrong to the international boundary, on the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway between Kamloops and Salmon Arm, on the Arrow and Kootenay lakes, Creston and Erickson, and in the Grand Forks valley on the. Kettle Valley railway that lies between the Arrow lakes and Okanagan lake. That comprises a total area 'of about forty thousand square miles.
The first carload of apples was shipped from the interior of British Columbia in 1903. In 1900 the total apple production of British Columbia was 240 boxes, and at the present time it is around six million boxes or over. This year there is a possibility, if the crop continues to develop according to present prospects, of a production of close to eight million boxes. Considering the time it takes to produce orchards, I think everyone will realize that the development has been very rapid indeed.
Originally the production was started to supply the home market of British Columbia and, later, the prairie markets. Production rapidly increased far beyond the needs of the local population, and when the prairie markets could not consume our products new fields were explored, until before the war apples were reaching all parts of the world. I am speaking of just prior to the war. At that time we sent about 40,000 boxes annually to South Africa and 100,000 boxes to South America; we sent 50,000 boxes to Egypt,
130,000	boxes to the United States, but our best overseas market was Great Britain which took from two to two and a half million boxes. During the war these normal marketing arrangements were disturbed, but I am glad to say that there is evidence at the present time of our former customers being anxious again to receive British Columbia fruit. It is amazing how quickly that situation has developed. From the heads of our organizations I understand that we are getting inquiries from various countries of Europe, South America, Australia, South Africa, in fact all of our former customers
