who are in position to buy apples at this time, although owing to their circumstances they are asking for limited quantities.
Years ago we were under the impression that unified control of the fruit industry could be obtained by voluntary effort, but in 1925 and 1926 the weaknesses of the voluntary effort became apparent to all those directly concerned with organizing the industry. Then a drive for legislative action and assistance was commenced. As a result of that drive the natural product marketing act of British Columbia was placed on the statute books. No doubt hon. members have heard the legislation condemned on the score that its coercive powers savours of regimentation and robs the individual of his rights. Time does not permit me to go into that argument. It is sufficient for me to say that it is based solely upon the rule of the majority. The only type of legislation we have ever asked for is the type of legislation which provides that when seventy-five per cent of the producers of any commodity wish to join together, then all producers of that commodity must abide by the rules and regulations set out in the act as a result of the decision of the majority. I think everyone will agree that a seventy-five per cent majority is democratic to the last degree. If agriculture is ever to come into its own from our point of view, one of the outstanding requisites is unification of action in the marketing sphere, provincially, nationally and internationally. To this principle the fruit growers, the vegetable growers and the poultry producers of my constituency adhere.
I wish to deal briefly with certain aspects of the marketing question. Under present conditions, in the preparation of our crop for marketing extensive facilities have been provided in the way of warehouses, graders and general packinghouse equipment. We must deliver high quality, attractively packed fruit if we are to hold our markets and extend them. I have often heard it suggested that too much expense is incurred in the packing of our fruit, and that we should ship it loose in containers direct from the orchard to the consumer.
I am going to deal with this aspect of the matter for a minute or two because I myself receive letters from the prairies suggesting that this would be the most economical and cheapest way to handle our crop. I can understand that point of view, but I should like to outline some of the difficulties. For the information of the committee let me say that first our fruit has to be graded so as to eliminate insect infested, diseased and deformed fruit. Then it has to be checked over on the graders to be properly sized. The reason is that all these
various markets demand a particular size or a particular variety of fruit. I shall illustrate it this way: South America will take only extra and fancy Delicious running 72 to 138 per box. Egypt will take only Newtons and Delicious running 72 to 125 to the box. South Africa demands Jonathons and McIntosh, running 138 to 216 to the box. The south of England prefers apples running 163 to 234 to the box; Li verpool, 150 to 180 to the box; Glasgow, 138 to 163 to the box; Montreal, 150 to 180 to the box, and Toronto, 80 to 125.
That is an interesting point. You always find that the large cities in the old country, and apparently in this country as demonstrated by the figures for Montreal, like the small apples. That is because when poor people want to give each of the kids an apple before they go to school, they like to buy a box containing a large number of apples, because a box goes much farther. It is interesting to note that Toronto buys the largest sizes and most select apples, 80 to 125, so it is obvious that our good friends in Toronto go in for the more expensive apples. Some of our Canadian markets want apples in grade C; others want nothing but the best in extras and fancies. Therefore to get the sizes and grades preferred by the different markets at home and abroad we are almost compelled to pack the whole crop. I am sure that is an aspect of the situation which is not appreciated by many people on the prairies. Harvesting the bulk of the apple crop usually takes a period of six weeks, but it takes twelve months to sell the crop, so that expensive cold storage facilities have been built. At the present time we have cold storage in British Columbia for approximately five million boxes. That represents an immense investment in the fruit industry.
In regard to the sale of the crop I think the growers are at the present time getting a reasonable proportion of the consumer's dollar; but the fruit industry is in a peculiar position. A great deal of its perishable product has to be marketed over a short period of time, and one has to sell through the channels established for the handling of that crop. A wholesaler or jobber cannot keep going by selling apples or tree fruits alone. He has to handle citrus fruits and other commodities to cover his overhead. So that this handling of fruit from the producer to the consumer is a complex and difficult question. I think I can safely say that, without a doubt, experience has proved the value of the natural products marketing act, and the system of central selling organized under its protection, to the fruit growers of British Columbia and the com-

munity as a whole. In saying that, I mean it has benefited both the producer and the consumer.
I am going to deal briefly with the conditions that existed before the act -was passed, and with conditions at the present time. Mind you, the federal act might not be necessary if we sold all our apples in British Columbia, but we do not. We have to sell a great deal of our crop in other provinces and abroad, and that is why we need the protection of the proposed act.
Before the provincial act was passed we had internal competition, and the fruit grower received a most unfair proportion of the consumer's dollar. We had maldistribution of the crop to the Canadian market, through the practice of selling on consignment. I know in my own district, before we had unified control, our packing house would ship a carload to a certain town, and perhaps half a dozen other packing houses would do the same thing. As a result, a small town on the prairies would have possibly three or four cars of apples roll in the same day, when one car would be sufficient, while another town would be without fruit. Then we had large losses through trade abuses, such as excessive rebates. That was a serious condition before this act was passed. We had a high percentage of bad debts. We had an uninformed public, with little knowledge of varieties or suitable seasons, and we had an unfair division of the Canadian and export markets. All the powerful people were grabbing the domestic market and leaving to somebody else the export market, which of course is less profitable. Then we had a lack of coordination within the industry, which prevented development of the flexibility necessary to meet changing conditions or to enable us to cooperate satisfactorily with a government programme.
Those were the conditions which existed before the act came into force. Since the passing of the natural products marketing act and organized selling under the direction of the tree fruit board and Tree Fruits Limited, we have first, a return to the producer of the greatest possible share of the consumer's dollar under present circumstances and conditions. Looking at the question from the point of view of the national interest I believe the fruit growers of British Columbia are reasonably satisfied with the prices they are obtaining to-day.
Second, we now have a planned distribution on the western Canadian and other markets. We own and control Canadian Fruit Distributors, and the whole distribution of the western Canadian market is planned so that marketing may be efficiently organized.

Third, we now have fair dealings within the trade and the elimination of trade abuses. For instance, prior to the Natural Products Marketing Act, claims made by wholesalers for damaged fruit, particularly on the prairie market, averaged $17 a car. To-day these claims have been reduced to less than $2 a car. That is because we have our own inspection service and can investigate any complaint made.
Fourth, we now have an almost complete elimination of bad debts; and this is a most interesting feature. Since the act came into force Tree Fruits Limited has marketed between $100,000,000 and $110,000,000 worth of tree fruits. A normal business concern allows one to one and a half per cent loss for bad debts. That would mean, under the old conditions, that we would have lost around $1,000,000 in bad debts. Up to the first of this month, after marketing that large volume of fruit, we have lost in bad debts only $163. That is what planned, cooperative marketing does for the producer.
Fifth, owing to coordinated publicity and advertising, we now have an informed buying public. People know when to buy Delicious, when to buy Wealthies, when to buy McIntosh, when to buy Gravensteins. They are informed as to the value of the apple they intend to purchase, and the best use to make of it.
Sixth, we have a planned division of the Canadian and export markets. All the shippers, whether they are cooperative organizations, semi-cooperative or joint stock, have to take their proportion of the domestic market and the export market, and we now have a planned division of those markets.
Seventh, we have a complete coordination throughout the whole industry which makes it possible to meet to the best advantage any given situation, and to cooperate effectively with any government programme. When, owing to war conditions, the government was faced with difficulties, it entrusted their solution in British Columbia and Nova Scotia to organizations which, I am sure the minister will admit, rendered an entirely satisfactory performance, organizations which can do just as effective a job in time of peace. In our opinion the best possible chance of satisfactorily implementing the government's agricultural prices support legislation will be with the cooperation of the producers in the industry concerned, under a national natural products marketing act. In fairness, I must say that during the critical period of our organization and the critical war period, we were most fortunate in British Columbia in having as members of the tree fruit board and Tree

Fruits Limited men of exceptionally high principles and outstanding ability, willing to work unceasingly for the cooperative principle and on behalf of the growers they were elected to represent. We were most fortunate in that respect. .
In the few moments during which I have discussed this matter, I think I have proved that the Natural Product Marketing Act has been of great assistance to the fruit industry in British Columbia, and that under the provisions of the act the producers are providing fruit for the consumers at fair prices under present circumstances. As I have said before, we are convinced that if the producer is to be protected we must forge that missing link, a national natural products marketing act. The tree fruit growers of British Columbia pioneered the provincial act. They have been the pioneers in advocating for several years a national act of this type. They are simply asking the government to develop in the federal field what has proved so successful in the provincial field. Hon. members will remember that the federal act passed in the early thirties was declared ultra vires of dominion powers by the privy council. It will be remembered that the federal act passed in the early thirties was declared ultra vires of dominion powers, by the privy council, and the fruit growers of British Columbia have given a great deal of study to this matter in an effort to draft an act that would not be ultra vires. The Canadian federation of agriculture has endorsed the draft act and in their brief presented to the government on March 28, 1946, expressed a desire for federal marketing legislation on this basis.
Before concluding, I should like to read from the Canadian federation of agriculture brief, where it states:
We desire to express appreciation to your government for the substantial progress made in applying a policy of long-term contracts or floor prices assured a number of years in advance. This is in line with the views of the Canadian federation of agriculture and incidentally in harmony with the fundamental theme of our recent annual meeting.
To carry such a policy into effect successfully, will require orderly production and a regularity of flow of products concerned in export trade to market to meet the needs of importing countries. Unorganized and haphazard marketing methods will not do it. Producers could make a valuable contribution to a national marketing programme in respect to some products if federal legislation were provided to enable them to undertake it. Most of the provinces now have legislation which permits the producers to develop and qperate plans for marketing within their respective provinces. These have proven successful in practically all cases and at the same time are recognized as being in the general interest. But producers are blocked completely from coordinating their efforts with fellow producers in other provinces for interprovincial and export movement of their products because supplementary federal legislation is not yet available to them. There is a widespread national demand from our producers for such legislation and since the close of the war particularly it is becoming more and more insistent.
It should be pointed out that in at least one province in Canada, producer marketing plans which have been in operation under the War Measures Act, and now the Emergency Powers Act will become absolutely ineffective even provincially, without federal legislation such as we are now requesting.
Hon. members would be well advised to secure a copy of the draft act which was originally drafted by the fruit interests in British Columbia, submitted to the Canadian federation of agriculture, gone over again, finally accepted in final form by the federation, and then submitted to the government. I shall not read the whole of it, but I should like to place on record one brief section which deals with purpose and intent. It states:
The purpose and intent of this act is to provide in respect to interprovincial trade in Canada and in export trade, for the improvement of methods and practices of marketing of natural products, and for the promotion, control, regulation, or prohibition, of the marketing of natural products, in any or all respects and in whole or in part,
I just wish to emphasize again that our people are anxious to see this type of legislation in the federal field, as I said before, to forge the missing link between provincial and international' arrangements.
I urge that hon. members give some study to this question. We in British Columbia are firmly of the opinion that if we are to assure the orderly marketing of farm products in the future at fair and stable prices, we must have a national natural products marketing act as the link between provincial legislation and international arrangements. I have, and the fruit growers in my constituency, as wrell as fruit growers in British Columbia as a whole, have great faith in this type of legislation, because it depends for its success upon local and cooperative action, and involves the people concerned in the administration and the direction of their own affairs. That is what I like about it. This type of legislation permits the development of large-scale planning under the control of the people themselves. It is democratic in principle, democratic in action and, I am sure, has been proven to work to the advantage of the community as a whole. It will move the latent pioneer spirit of the past into action for the requirements of the future.
I should like the minister to express his opinion of the draft act presented to him by the Canadian federation of agriculture, and of the principles of marketing outlined therein.

Mr. Chairman, at this point in the discussion of the estimates for the Department of Agriculture I wish to say a few words on behalf of the primary producers in British Columbia. I find myself fully in agreement with the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West. I fully realize ^that, so far as agriculture in British Columbia is concerned, we have not reached the point of development that has been reached in the prairie provinces. However, with the building of 'the necessary railways to provide an outlet for the British Columbia-Peace River block, that situation will correct itself to some extent.
The constituency of Kootenay East, which I have the honour to represent, contains some fairly large agricultural areas, with their usual problems and needs. I might mention the Columbia river valley, the Creston valley fruit district and the range lands in the southeast corner of the province.

The setting up of a provincial marketing board has already been achieved in British Columbia, as mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West, and it has met with a fair degree of success in its work.
Then, too, the British Columbia fruit growers' association has united in the setting up of the British Columbia fruit marketing board. They, too, are doing good work, but over the years some weaknesses have manifested themselves which call for correction.
The farmers in my constituency who live fairly close to the British Columbia-Alberta boundary complain from time to time of Alberta surplus supplies being sold in British Columbia below our cost of production. It was at this point that our provincial marketing board fell down in that it could not control interprovincial trade. Therefore a dominion marketing board or a national marketing board is necessary to control the organized marketing of our agricultural products. To show that what I am advocating is a live issue, I should like to quote a press report in the Vancouver Sun which bears the date line of Victoria, April 11. It reads:
Hart wip urge Ottawa market law.
The British Columbia legislature to-day passed a resolution asking Premier Hart to urge on Ottawa authorities next month the need for federal legislation to control organized marketing of agricultural products.
The question was raised by J. H. Corsbie (C.C.F., Peace River), who said there is need for a dominion marketing act to make provincial marketing legislation fully effective in dealing with interprovincial trade.
Mention has already been made of the dominion marketing act which was passed in 1935 by the Bennett government and which was declared to be ultra vires of the powers of the federal government. I sincerely hope the minister will give serious consideration to the setting up of a dominion marketing board.

This matter has been an issue, not only since the hon. member for Melfort came to the house but at a time when most of us who are now in the house were not here. As the hon. member knows, this was a matter of live discusion during the thirties. At that time an act was passed which was presumed to do what is now being asked for. That act was taken to the supreme court and then to the privy council where it was declared to be ultra vires. I am not a constitutional lawyer either, but I take it that the members of the privy council are and they decided that that act was not constitutional.
It may be possible to draft an act which is constitutional, but I find it most difficult to believe that that is possible under our constitution. That does not mean that the constitution cannot be amended, but I would think it would be most difficult to draft even concurrent legislation that would be declared by the courts to be intra vires. The previous legislation was I believe, drafted most carefully with the thought in mind that it might be declared ultra vires. That act was in effect when I came to Ottawa and we. operated under it for a number of months. However, it was declared to be ultra vires and we have not since acted under it.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has suggested that I express an opinion with regard to the model act which was drafted, I believe in British Columbia, and presented to the Canadian federation of agriculture and by that federation to the government in the year just preceding the war. As Minister of Agriculture,
I took the matter to the government and it was discussed there. I had the government's policy with regard to it announced in the first year of the war, which policy is on record in Hansard. That policy was to affect the period of the war, and it was stated that further consideration would not be given to the matter until the end of the war.
To state in as few words as possible the position taken by the government, it was simply this. We had entered upon the war, and during the war period it would be absolutely necessary for the government to set up any boards that were necessary to take control of the marketing of farm products. Those boards would be operated by the government on behalf of the people of Canada and on behalf of those engaged in the war in order to assist in the prosecution of the war. We thought that could be most effectively done by the government operating under the War Measures Act. That is what we have since been doing, and the success of apple marketing during the war period has been partly due to the fact that we have had an arrangement with the apple producers and the tree fruit board right from the first year of the war. Under that agreement the government has taken possession of any surplus product we have had. That has been canned or' dehydrated and sometimes given away, but at all times the producer of apples was guaranteed a certain set return for his product.
The growers appreciated it.

The growers have expressed their appreciation on many occasions. I think we have had less criticism from the apple growers of Canada throughout the whole war period than from any other group. That action was taken in the first year of the war and was continued right through. It resulted in our paying out perhaps more per farmer engaged in the apple industry than we have paid out on behalf of any other group of farmers in Canada. When you talk about two or three million dollars to assist a branch of the industry, let us say in Nova Scotia, it does not sound very large as compared with other expenditures that are made, but there are only four or five thousand apple producers in Nova Scotia. When you spend two million dollars in order to promote the interests of four or five thousand producers and of those assisting in the marketing and processing of the product it figures out to a higher level per person involved than is the case even with the enormous amounts that have been expended in connection with wheat growing in

western Canada where we have spent in the neighbourhood of a few hundred millions, but the number of farmers engaged is very much greater.
The minister will admit that that is because of the loss of export markets.

I agree that that was the reason for the action taken in the first instance. The British government said in the first year of the war: We do not want any apples at all. I would remind hon. members of that fact when they sometimes speak of fruit as an important food product that would help people who are starving. But the British said: We do not want to utilize any shipping space for the shipment of apples because of their low food value. We all know that that is true. The apple is used not particularly for preventing starvation but for purposes we all understand. I think we all enjoy apples, and most people throughout the world do when they have an opportunity of getting them. But at a time when it was necessary to do everything to prosecute the war successfully the British said that they did not want apples at all. We naturally had to do something about the situation, and the only thing we could do was to guarantee a certain return to the producers until such time as they could market their product.
We had less difficulty with the apple crop in British Columbia than we had with the apple crop of Nova Scotia, for reasons more or less obvious. The apple crop of British Columbia has its market next door in the prairie provinces, for at least a considerable portion of the crop. Might I suggest to the apple growers of British Columbia that something happened during the war which might work out most beneficially to the apple producers of British Columbia and probably other parts of Canada, if the idea is used to the fullest possible extent? During the war we developed to a greater extent than ever before the process of dehydrating fruit and vegetables. One of the difficulties in marketing British Columbia apples on the prairies is that the temperature sometimes gets down to forty below in November, and anyone who knows anything about transporting apples on the prairies knows that if you start out from your town or village with a barrel or box of apples when it is forty below the apples will not be of much value when you get four or five miles away from town.
How often does it get forty below in November?

My hon. friend will probably find out in a year or two. It has been thirty below on the prairies in October, and even that temperature will freeze apples. The position is that if you attempt to take apples out in their natural state on the prairies you have difficulties in the winter months. But dehydration was developed greatly during the war to the point where apples can now be put on a shelf in any part of western Canada and fdrty below will do them no harm whatsoever. Dehydration dries them down to the same moisture content as wheat, so that they can be put anywhere and carted about from one place to another and consumed the whole year round.
I had some dried apples from Nova Scotia presented to me just at the beginning of the war. They had been dried three years prior to the time they were presented to me. I took them home and had them cooked, and you could not distinguish the product from apples picked fresh off the tree. I realize that what made it impossible to carry that further was the cost of dehydration. But we have gone a long way during the war, and if we will only take advantage of our experience a great deal can be done to assist in the marketing of the apple crop. Much of that we learned because we were required to process products during the war, partly to take care of them over a long period and partly to feed the troops and others who required different products at different places where storage was necessary.
So far as the act itself which has been proposed is concerned, I wish to state only this. During the war we have used boards. We had a meat board, a dairy board, a wheat board, a special products board and a fruit tree board, and under these boards we have handled most of our farm products during the war. We still have those boards. In addition, we have an agreement with Britain on pork products extending down to 1948. We have an agreement on cheese extending down to 1948. We have an agreement under consideration for wheat extending down to the end of the 1949 crop, which agreement in all probability will eventually be signed. We have also an agreement with regard to canned milk. When one takes all these products into consideration -and others I might name, it will be realized that exactly the same condition exists in relation to them down to the end of these agreements as did exist during the war.
We have these boards, operated by the government it is true, but operated on behalf of all the people of Canada, to handle the exportation of our surplus farm products whether they come from a private organiza-

in British Columbia. When I was a schoolboy I used to learn some things that I never understood the meaning of until much later. One of the things I learned was that nature provides, through the texture of leaves, bark and other parts of plants, against evaporation in dry climates. I never did associate that with apples until I came east ten years ago to take tire position I now occupy.
I knew from my experience on the farm as a boy in Ontario where apples were grown, that when you put apples on the shelves in the cellar and left them there for use during the winter months they shriveled up very quickly. The British Columbia apple does not do that, not with the same readiness. If you leave it long enough the moisture will evaporate from it, and there is a simple explanation of it when one has occasion to get the explanation. It is associated with the fact that apples in Ontario have to be kept with greater care than they do if they are produced in British Columbia. In the Okanagan valley the apples are produced under irrigation. The air is very dry, and the result is that the skin on the apple does not permit of evaporation easily. It is nature's way of seeing that evaporation does not take place. The pores in the skin of the apple produced under these conditions do not give off moisture as freely as they do in a moist climate like Ontario, and it is even more moist over in the area in Britain in which the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar lived. That might have something to do with his suggestion that the apples there are not as good even as they are here. They are produced under different climatic conditions.
Those who do take care of apples, and do it properly, in Ontario, are able to overcome that difficulty through cold storage facilities that are made for the storage of apples. In our boyhood days we did not have the cold storage that we have to-day, and the result was that the apples went on the market in a different form from what British Columbia or even well' cared for Ontario apples do.
Associated with that is this further fact. A very small proportion of the apples of Ontario and Quebec need to be exported. They have their market right next door to them. We grade the apples which are exported, but there are some years when they have a very good crop and no apples are exported from Ontario and Quebec at all; they are all exported from Nova Scotia and British Columbia. The apples of Nova Scotia and British Columbia have to meet the grading regulations that are put on by the federal department, Apples marketed in Ottawa, if they are

I should like to ask a few questions with regard to the purchasing of horses by the Netherlands and the French governments. There was some discussion on this matter at the last session, and the minister indicated then that the methods being used in western Canada were not satisfactory. He- said that he intended to change that method and purchase through the municipalities there, or at least use the municipalities for the assembling of the horses for purchase. Representations were made to the government by the various horse breeders' associations in the west that they would prefer to have the purchasing done through the special products marketing board direct from the farmers on behalf of the French purchasing commission which was in Canada purchasing these horses. Could the minister give us some information with regard to the matter? How many horses have been purchased by the French government? What method is being employed? Are they buying direct through the trade, or is the government assembling the horses? Just what method is being used at the present time? Could the minister give the average price that is being paid by the French purchasing commission for the horses that they are purchasing?
["Mr. Gardiner.]

Last session there were discussions in regard to the marketing of horses; I believe the matter was brought up on the floor of the house by the hon. member for Wood Mountain. I do not know that there was any considerable dissatisfaction with the plan followed, other than that there was not a market for all types of horses, and perhaps in regard to the system of asking farmers, many of whom were not able to determine from the circulars put out just what type of horse was required, to bring in their horses and take their chance on selling them-perhaps that did not work out so satisfactorily in view of the fact that too many of them had to take their horses home again.
Two agreements were drawn up; one had been signed. That was with the government of the Netherlands. It covered the delivery of
5,000	horses, beginning a year ago last spring and continuing to next October. When I was in Europe in January I took the trouble to see those on the other side, particularly in the Netherlands, who had been handling the horses. They said they were perfectly satisfied with the horses they had received, as to both quality and price, but they said they did not want any more. Of the 5,000 they had received some 2,200. I asked why they did not want any more, and they said they were going to be exporting horses within twelve months. They told me that the reports they had at the end of the war, on the basis on which they entered into the agreement to buy 5,000 horses from Canada, were not in accordance with the facts as they later developed. They had far more horses in the country than they thought, and they said that within twelve months they would be exporting horses and therefore did not want to buy any more from us. I did not tell them we were going to force them to carry out their contract. We just have not shipped them any more horses. Up to that time they had bought 2,200; since then they have not taken any more, and under the circumstances I do not believe we should insist on the contract being carried out. So that deals with the situation as far as the Netherlands is concerned.
In France it was a different situation. As hon. members know, the French governments were changing very rapidly in January, and we had not signed a contract with them. We never have had a signed contract. The contract was drawn upon the basis that they would buy 35,000 horses over a period of time and would advance a certain amount of money for each horse purchased. We undertook to return any cash that was not required in order to purchase and ship the horse. Under that arrangement, which was never signed, we sent,

I think, something over 2,500 horses last year, for which the farmers obtained an average price of just three cents under $100. The actual figure was $99.97, after making allowance for the losses that had to be taken by reason of certain horses not being suitable. The farmers received that amount of money, and there was some money left over of the total that had been advanced.
Was that f.o.b. the shipping point?

That was $100 to the farmer himself. They cost more than that, of course, at Montreal, from where they were shipped. One of the conditions that developed in that connection was that some people apparently got the notion that they could handle these horses more satisfactorily through local organizations, that is, private organizations. I discussed the matter with the French minister of agriculture in Paris. He said he was of the opposite opinion and thought the agreement should be signed and carried out as it had been discussed originally. Others, however, had different views, and he did not have full control over the purchasing or marketing of the horses. While I was in England last year, a delegation from France arrived here to buy horses. They entered into negotiations with private interests to purchase horses on somewhat the same basis that had been discussed previously with the government. One of the reasons given by some people who were discussing the matter -not by the minister in France-was that in some of the discussions which took place in this house the statement was made that you could buy horses in different constituencies of eastern Canada for $30 and $40, so that naturally they asked why they should be paying something over $100. Well, one can understand that when statements of that kind go to the people who are providing the money some of them begin to wonder whether or not that is the case. I understand that the arrangement they now have is one under which they agree to put up approximately the same amount for each horse that they had agreed to put up with the government, but the buyers who go out to look for the horses are in a different position from that of the government buyers. We had no means of disposing of horses other than to the French and Belgian governments. The ordinary dealer may buy horses for any trade whatever. He goes into a community, buys a carload of horses and probably gets them at an average price of $60-the price at which they tell me horses can be bought in western Canada-to be shipped to Toronto or Montreal. No one knows whether all the horses purchased are of the right quality to go to France or Belgium or wherever it may be. They only know the buyer purchases a carload of horses and pays a certain price. We have checked some of these shipments. I would not say we have checked them all; we had no particular right to check them all. This is a deal made absolutely between the French government and the local buyers, most of them in Toronto and Montreal.
But financed out of our loan.

Perhaps financed out of the loan we made to France, but in any event we put no strings on that loan except to specify that a certain amount must be spent in .this country. They buy goods in their own way and no doubt finance their purchases with money lent to them by Canada. On those we did check, however, I had a report from Mr. MacCallum, who is the nearest thing we have to an expert on live stock, indicating that on one shipment the amount the farmer received for the horses that actually went to France was within a few cents of the amount he received for the horses we shipped last fall. Recently I have heard another suggestion that a carload of horses was bought,
I think in the neighbourhood of Prince Rupert, at $40 per horse. I have asked for a check to be made to see if we can determine what percentage of those horses went to France or whether any at all went to that country. They may not have gone to France at all; but the horses that were actually loaded on the boat in the one check I made brought the farmer approximately the same amount he received under the plan we put into effect last fall.

You do not know how
the French government fares in these deals, in comparison?

Well, within the last week I had in my office two representatives of the French government, with whom I discussed the matter, and they said they were satisfied with what they were getting. At the present time they are asking for a higher standard horse, a 1,500 pound horse as against the 1,350 pound horse that was being asked for by France last fall. They say they are getting good horses; they are satisfied with them and with the treatment they are receiving. So that I would hesitate to step into an understanding of that kind which is satisfactory to both sides.

I shall explain it. The position is that we have been paying for many years a subsidy which amounts to 30 per cent of the cost of constructing the plant. Half the 30 per cent is paid in the year the plant is constructed and the other half is divided equally over the next four years. The payments are made conditionally; no matter who constructs the plant, whether it be a private individual, a company, or a cooperative, the condition is that the plant must allow the public the services of that plant. The individual cannot utilize the plant for his own purposes if he accepts this grant; if he does not accept it he can do what he likes with his cold storage. Then we have certain rights in connection with the rates which are charged. We simply keep a check on them, and if those we assisted were charging unreasonable rates they would be checked up on that. There is an understanding that they must charge rates which are satisfactory to the department.
What is the situation with regard to these small cold storage plants which are being erected at the present time throughout the west?
Plants which, I understand, have lockers in them?
Yes, a locker system.

The regulation is that a plant which receives this assistance can have only 15 per cent of locker space, which is one way of enforcing the idea that the plant must be open to the general public. I have been arguing the point a little recently with officials in the department as to whether that should
[Mr. McKay.1
be changed. I said that conditions have changed considerably, and particularly out in our part of the country. It is the most useful kind of cold storage, I think, that can be put in in villages and towns where you have not any reason for having these large services such as you have in big cities. That matter is under discussion. Personally I am favourable to the suggestion that the assistance under this act should be applied to this class of storage plant, but up to the moment it has not been done.
At the moment none of these has received any assistance?
No, not up to the moment, if they have more than 15 per cent given over to locker space.

This vote is referred to on page 93 of the main estimates and several pages later, containing the details. I went through them some time ago and I noticed there were not any subsidies listed for Saskatchewan. Why are these not listed in the detailed explanation?
Those which are listed in the statement are only those which are affected by the grants which are in these votes, and these have not yet been made.
You were speaking of the Moose Jaw and Regina grants.

I understood the question to be whether there were any in Saskatchewan that have been given assistance. I have just given one for Kingston which did receive assistance. Could the minister indicate whether in the supplementary estimates we might expect some grants for these smaller cold storage plants which are providing locker service? There will be money in the supplementary estimates, as there always is, for any applications received between the time these estimates are made up and the time the house closes. But I think we would require to change the legislation in order to bring in the type of cold storage we are discussing

What particular kind of organization must apply, or likely will apply, if you grant these small places the right to build locker plants?

A number have applied, and the organization I know best is the one in the second nearest town to where I myself live, that is in Abernethy. It is an organization of farmers, largely, and business people; they formed an association and built a cold storage locker plant, and they wrote here to see whether they were entitled to the grant. We informed them that under the legislation and the regulations as they now are they were not entitled to it.- I think maybe I had half a dozen such applications of that type from Saskatchewan.

I notice in the estimates there is $7,000 this year for Trenton cold storage, and there was $15,000 last year. The minister said this evening that subsidies are paid over a period of four years. This has beep going on for a number of years-more than four. How much has been paid out in subsidies to the Trenton cold storage warehouse?

The only explanation is that there have been extensions. If the plant were built twenty years ago it would get its first grant in*the first four years; but three or four years ago it may have added an extension on which it is entitled to the grant. I should say that a feature of the law is that any plant which gets a grant must apply before it starts its building operations. If that is not done, they are not entitled under the law to a grant. On a number of occasions, I would say probably a dozen times since I have been here, in ten years, we have had to bring in a special vote for some concerns which inadvertently broke that part of the law.
Do they submit their plans to you?

They submit their plans to us. First, they have to make a request to the department which is dealt with in the dairy branch. The dairy branch examine the existing situation, as to the need, and advise them at the time the application is made as 63260-125J
to whether on that basis it would be acceptable to the department. After that is done, they are required to build it up to a certain standard and live up to the other conditions which I mentioned a few moments ago.
The minister has dealt mostly with the grant part of it; but on what basis are the subsidies paid?
The only subsidy that is paid-you might call it a grant, or a subsidy-	,
You include that?

There is no subsidy. I am informed that there are a few instances where it was impossible for those applying to live up to the conditions of the act where a grant has been made apart from the subsidies that are paid under the conditions of the act, but there are only a few of them scattered over a long period of time.

The minister has partly answered the question I had intended to ask. Are these subsidies granted to all who apply, provided that they comply with the regulations, or are you limited by the appropriation or by any departmental regulations?

I think I can best-answer, that by saying that in the early stages of the act applications were made and were practically all accepted, but there was a period just prior to the war when cold storage was overbuilt. I believe it began in the period when Mr. Bennett was here, and it continued on to the first years that I was here down to war time when we had to check this whole situation carefully in different communities before agreeing to add to the cold storage. That continued for about two years of the war, and then it became evident that because of the enormous shipping of food products we had to have more cold storage. From then down to the present these have been passed almost automatically. If persons could live up to the conditions of the act and the cold storage were needed-and there were very few cases where it was not needed- it was passed almost automatically. At the moment I cannot recall any that have not been passed in recent years.

It was passed in 1907.

Could the minister tell us something about the honey production, what the marketing of honey is likely to be in the future? I believe there has been a big expansion in the production of honey in Saskatchewan -and other western provinces.

The 1945 honey crop was estimated at 30,683,000 pounds and valued at $4,946,000, or 11-8 per cent short of the 1944 crop, which was valued at $5,253,400. The average yield per colony was only fifty-nine pounds as compared with sixty-nine pounds in 1944, and the 1935-39 average of ninety-three pounds. The production has been down per colony. Adverse weather conditions in eastern Canada were responsible for the reduced total.	,
Increased interest in beekeeping evidenced since the outbreak of war continued during 1945, the total number of beekeepers rising to the record figure of 43,800 as compared with 40,700 in 1944, and the 1935-39 average of 26,860. The number of colonies of bees operated in 1945 was 524,100, as against 508,500 in 1944 and the 1935-39 average of 382,840. The demand for honey was heavy, despite rationing restrictions, and ceiling prices were maintained throughout the year.

Earlier the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar raised the question of the variation across the dominion in the quality of fruit. On a previous occasion I raised the question of variations in the quality of fruits and vegetables offered for sale in cans. Could the minister make some statement on what his department is doing so that a consumer who buys canned goods may have some guarantee in regard to quality? There has been a great variation in the qualities offered in different parts of Canada at different times. During the Stevens price spreads inquiry it was disclosed that there were some irregularities in connection with this trade. So that I should like the minister to explain what assurance the consumer has that canned goods being offered for sale have been inspected as to quality and quantity.

As I remember them, the Stevens reports criticized the great number of sizes of containers, and also criticized the quality to some extent. We have regulations which I think were brought in during the last year before we took over in 1935 and which, since that time, have been adjusted as a result of our experience. I believe we have regulations in that regard as strict as any that can be found anywhere.
How about fruits and vegetables canned in British Columbia; how do they compare with those canned in Ontario or the maritimes?

They are much the same. The standard is the same; the containers are of standard sizes, and the quality is good. There may be some difference in the quality of the different fruits in different years. In other words, some years weather conditions in Ontario make it difficult to produce the best quality fruits, and in other years you will find similar conditions with regard to certain other fruits in British Columbia. Tire product may not look to be as good, but it is at least supposed to be graded up to an equal standard.
What machinery have you to assure the consumer that Aylmer or Heinz or Campbell canned goods, first quality, are similar to those offered by other competitors?

The plants are all
specially inspected, but I must repeat that we should keep in mind in connection with these matters the fact that we have no control over fruit that is put up in Ontario for sale in Ontario. We control only fruit that may be exported from Ontario. A short time ago I made a statement for which one of the local newspapers took me to task. I said that the red gauze was being taken off peaches. That is a fact; the red gauze is being taken off peaches as far as we have any control over them, but we cannot control the marketing of peaches in Ontario which are grown in Ontario. Of course that was made perfectly plain at the time.

The minister would not have time to-night, but at the next sitting of the committee would he deal with a question which is of vital importance to fruit growers almost from coast to coast? It has to do with the importation of maraschino cherries, particularly Italian cherries, that have come or are likely to come into Canada because the ad valorem duty is very low. During the war a definite improvement was made in the production of maraschino cherries from both British Columbia and Ontario fruit, and a really beautiful product has been turned out. I know great fears are felt that this market may be lost. I believe we must say, to the credit of the growers and processors of this country, that they have turned out a product second to none. I know the minister would not have time to deal with the matter to-night, but at the next sitting of the committee would he review the situation and tell us the possibilities? Even if there should be need of subsidies, certainly some assistance should be given to the fruit growers and processors to protect their market, after they made such valiant attempts during the war years to

provide a Canadian product which had not been produced heretofore. Would the minister give us a full statement as to the possibilities of protecting that market in the interests of our fruit growers? It has grown to be an important market, and a wonderful product has been turned out.

I can say that what has been said in regard to the matter is in accordance with the facts as I know them. There has been a considerable development of this production, but I am afraid I cannot say anything about what will happen until the conclusion of the trade meeting which is to take place this summer. That meeting is being held for the purpose of taking restrictions off trade. I do not know whether we are going to advocate putting on any, but that is something which will have to be considered. I do not think I could say anything in that regard that would be helpful.

Could the minister assure us that these growers and processors who developed that industry during the war years will receive his support within the government when the question arises? I realize that this is a matter concerning duties and that sort of thing, which probably does not come within his department, but could be assure us of his support?
All I can say is that I am not a protectionist.

It is not a matter of protection; it is a matter of preventing a product from being dumped in this country from another country where there is quite a different standard of living. It js not a question of protection at all; it is a question of the survival of an industry which has been more or less perfected in Canada during the last few years.

It is Italian fruit; we may as well call a spade a spade. Here is a country that is likely to come in and take away the splendid market that has been developed in this country, and I think the minister should give the matter the fullest possible consideration.
My hon. friend has said it is dumping, and if that is so it cannot be done under the present law.
The dumping duty was taken off at the beginning of the war. Why should it not be reestablished?

To the best of my knowledge the United States has a duty of about ten cents a pound against the Italian cherries,

which prevents them from being dumped on that market; and I understand that the British market is closed to this product.
I believe our duty is 15 per cent plus two cents.

I think it is 17^ per cent.
